artboards.title: Supervising an agent, one run at a time
A release as a tray (not chosen)
A form with its own hero

annotations.text:
Shio's 23 migrated console screens are not drawn, and should not be: the shell and BENTO-AUTHORING already decided them, so an artboard would re-open a settled question.
These five are the ones this round invents, where the layout has real alternatives and the data model follows from the choice. Each says what it decides and names the direction it did not take.
The drawing is the cheap half. Every region on these five needs a row in a table that does not exist yet, which is what makes them worth settling before the backend is written.

A rejected direction is kept drawn, not deleted, so the next reader does not re-propose it and the argument against it survives with it.
The release tray is the one that needed drawing rather than a sentence: it reads perfectly well, and everything wrong with it is invisible on the screen itself.

Three decisions live on this page, and none of them is a component defect -- which is why no component change closes them.
The contract says adopt the shell before the pages. These artboards say what the shell is: what the header carries and in what order, who owns the reading column, and which surfaces --primary reaches.
The content is role-labelled on purpose. Routes and entity names belong to a product, never to this package.

Almost every screen is one of four shapes plus data: a detail is BentoEntityShell wrapping a form, a list is one BentoListPage call with a renderTile, a form with no entity behind it yet is BentoFormHero as the first child of its form, and a form beside its preview is BentoSplitPage under one hero.
The panel is the fifth thing and not a shape: a frosted box with no heading, for whatever a hero already named.
The last artboard is the same components on both grounds, because one look means one look twice.
